submission.natural_language_explanation: N1762+ is a line-start layout detector: it fires on the token that opens a new line of a non-prose, formatted document when that token carries no word content - a symbol token directly after a newline (table pipe, bracket, list dash, heading hash, comment slashes, bullet, rule characters, closing bracket) or the whitespace of an indentation run - and it fires most strongly when the line follows a blank line, so the newline that opens a blank line itself fires (~0.3 of max) as well. It is silent on words, including words at the start of a line, and on prose punctuation mid-sentence, and it is only weakly active (mostly under 0.25 of max) on the same symbol tokens when they appear mid-line.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Our review of the incident began on a rainy Tuesday, when the support team forwarded a transcript [attached] and a short note from the vendor (the same vendor we had used for years). The transcript showed that the first attempt returned 412 rows, the second returned 397 rows and the third returned 408 rows; nobody could explain the drift, and the engineer on call - who had joined the company in 2019 - wrote back that the difference was expected. We asked for the raw export, which arrived as a pipe-delimited file where the separator was a | character and the escape was a backslash; the fields included an invoice number like #7 and a status column that mixed values such as Open, Closed and Reopened. One row contained a stray bullet • in the middle of a description, another contained a stray pair of slashes // where a path should have been, and a third carried a long run of equals ============ inside a free-text comment. None of these artefacts were at the start of a line: each sat mid-row, between ordinary words, and the export had been generated by a script that wrote every record on a single line before joining the records with a semicolon. The team then tried to reproduce the counts by running grep | sort | uniq on the export, and the totals matched the vendor's numbers exactly, which suggested the drift came from the database, not from the file. A follow-up ticket (#4211) was opened, and the database team - after two days of silence - reported that a nightly job had been rebuilding an index while the export ran. The fix was simple: the job was rescheduled, the export was rerun, and the counts settled at 401 rows on three consecutive mornings. The incident closed without further comment, and the rainy Tuesday was never mentioned again. A copy of the export was later archived on a share whose path contained a doubled slash // in the middle of the folder name, and the archiving job, written by an intern who left the following month, kept a summary line that read total = 401 and a note that read invoice #7 reopened.
